steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proposing Projected Task-Specific Layers, a new backbone architecture for multi-task reinforcement learning in robot manipulation. Motivate the problem, explain where current multi-task approaches fall short, describe the architecture briefly and list our contributions.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation: complex manipulation tasks share primitives
  - examples: wiping kitchen surfaces in a busy restaurant, routing cables in a datacenter, screwing parts in manufacturing assembly
  - tasks differ but are composed of similar manipulation primitives
  - humans scaffold on primitives intuitively; hard for robots trained on individual, specific tasks
  - multi-task RL -> more general-purpose robotics; efficient learning across similar tasks, shared structure -> better policy
- Why multi-task learning is still hard
  - needs careful task choice + balanced sampling; may not improve learning anyway
  - learning-based approaches for complex manipulation may generalize to unseen tasks, but hard to scale
  - recent work: use shared task structures
  - most approaches: single shared policy for all tasks -> may not represent variations between tasks
- Our proposal: PTSL
  - new backbone: large shared fully-connected policy + low-rank task-specific layers (Fig. 1)
  - after each layer, hidden states of shared and low-rank task-specific policy combined -> expressive of different tasks
  - evaluated standalone and on top of CARE (Context-based Representation) encoder: text descriptions of task as metadata, projects a mixture of encodings
- Main contributions
  - PTSL architecture: low-rank task-specific layers on top of each layer of shared backbone
  - outperforms CARE (current state-of-the-art) on MT10 and MT50 Goal-conditioned benchmarks, Meta-World
  - shared projection: more sample efficient, can improve learning on individual tasks
  - insights into intermediate architectures sharing an embedding space between task-specific layers and backbone

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Robots are wanted in a lot of real-world use cases that involve complex manipulation, for example wiping different kitchen surfaces in a busy restaurant, routing cables in a datacenter, or screwing parts in a manufacturing assembly. These tasks are different from each other, but they are often made up of similar manipulation primitives. Humans recognize these primitives intuitively and build on them to do different tasks. This is hard for robots, since robots are often only trained on individual, specific tasks. Letting robots reason through several related tasks with multi-task reinforcement learning can unlock more general-purpose robotics, because it allows efficient learning across similar tasks and the shared structure of the tasks can be used to learn a policy that performs better.

But multi-task learning often needs a careful choice of tasks and balanced sampling, and even with that it does not always improve learning. For complex manipulation, learning-based approaches may generalize over unseen tasks but they can still be difficult to scale successfully. Recent work has argued that learning methods should use shared task structures. But most approaches still learn one single shared policy that is used for all of the tasks, and this may not represent the variations between tasks well enough.

- Our proposal: PTSL
  - new backbone: large shared fully-connected policy + low-rank task-specific layers (Fig. 1)
  - after each layer, hidden states of shared and low-rank task-specific policy combined -> expressive of different tasks
  - evaluated standalone and on top of CARE (Context-based Representation) encoder: text descriptions of task as metadata, projects a mixture of encodings
- Main contributions
  - PTSL architecture: low-rank task-specific layers on top of each layer of shared backbone
  - outperforms CARE (current state-of-the-art) on MT10 and MT50 Goal-conditioned benchmarks, Meta-World
  - shared projection: more sample efficient, can improve learning on individual tasks
  - insights into intermediate architectures sharing an embedding space between task-specific layers and backbone

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Robots are wanted in a lot of real-world use cases that involve complex manipulation, for example wiping different kitchen surfaces in a busy restaurant, routing cables in a datacenter, or screwing parts in a manufacturing assembly. These tasks are different from each other, but they are often made up of similar manipulation primitives. Humans recognize these primitives intuitively and build on them to do different tasks. This is hard for robots, since robots are often only trained on individual, specific tasks. Letting robots reason through several related tasks with multi-task reinforcement learning can unlock more general-purpose robotics, because it allows efficient learning across similar tasks and the shared structure of the tasks can be used to learn a policy that performs better.

But multi-task learning often needs a careful choice of tasks and balanced sampling, and even with that it does not always improve learning. For complex manipulation, learning-based approaches may generalize over unseen tasks but they can still be difficult to scale successfully. Recent work has argued that learning methods should use shared task structures. But most approaches still learn one single shared policy that is used for all of the tasks, and this may not represent the variations between tasks well enough.

We propose instead a new backbone architecture, which we call Projected Task-Specific Layers (PTSL). It combines a large, shared fully-connected policy with low-rank task-specific layers, as shown in Fig. 1. After each layer, the hidden state of the shared policy and the hidden state of the low-rank task-specific policy are combined, and this is what makes PTSL expressive of different tasks. We evaluate PTSL as a standalone backbone and also on top of the Context-based Representation (CARE) encoder, which uses text descriptions of the task as metadata to project a mixture of encodings.

Our main contributions are:

- We propose PTSL, an architecture for deep multi-task reinforcement learning that adds low-rank task-specific layers on top of each layer of a shared backbone.
- Our results with PTSL are better than CARE, which is the current state-of-the-art, on the MT10 and on the MT50 Goal-conditioned benchmarks from Meta-World.
- Our results also suggest that multi-task learning with a shared projection is more sample efficient and that it can improve learning on individual tasks.
- Finally, our results give some insights into the benefits of intermediate architectures that share an embedding space between task-specific layers and a backbone.

But multi-task learning often needs a careful choice of tasks and balanced sampling, and even with that it does not always improve learning. For complex manipulation, learning-based approaches may generalize over unseen tasks [5] but they can still be difficult to scale successfully [6,7]. Recent work has argued that learning methods should use shared task structures [8,9]. But most approaches still learn one single shared policy that is used for all of the tasks, and this may not represent the variations between tasks well enough [6,10].

We propose instead a new backbone architecture, which we call Projected Task-Specific Layers (PTSL). It combines a large, shared fully-connected policy with low-rank task-specific layers, as shown in Fig. 1. steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Complex manipulation is common in a number of desirable real-world robotic use cases, such as wiping various kitchen surfaces in a busy restaurant, routing cables in a datacenter, or screwing parts in a manufacturing assembly. While these individual tasks are different, they are often composed of similar manipulation primitives. Humans intuitively recognize and scaffold upon these primitives to implement different tasks, but it is challenging for robots, which are often only trained on individual, specific tasks, to do the same. Enabling robots to reason through multiple related tasks with multi-task reinforcement learning [1] can unlock more general-purpose robotics, allowing efficient learning across similar tasks and using their shared structure to learn a better performing policy [2,3,4].

However, multi-task learning often requires a careful choice of tasks and balanced sampling, and even then may not always improve learning. For complex manipulation, learning-based approaches may generalize over unseen tasks [5] but can still be difficult to scale successfully [6,7]. Recent work has argued that learning methods should use shared task structures [8,9], but most approaches still learn a single shared policy used across all tasks, which may not adequately represent variations between tasks [6,10].

Instead, we propose a new backbone architecture, the Projected Task-Specific Layers (PTSL), which combines a large, shared fully-connected policy with low-rank task-specific layers as shown in Fig. 1. After each layer, the hidden states from the shared policy and the low-rank task-specific policy are combined, which makes PTSL expressive of different tasks. We evaluate PTSL as a standalone backbone and on top of the Context-based Representation (CARE [4]) encoder, which leverages text descriptions of the task as metadata to project a mixture of encodings.

The main contributions of this work are:

- We propose the PTSL architecture for deep multi-task reinforcement learning, which adds low-rank task-specific layers on top of each layer of a shared backbone.
- Our results with PTSL outperform CARE [4], the current state-of-the-art, on both the MT10 and MT50 Goal-conditioned benchmarks from Meta-World [11].
- Further, our results suggest that multi-task learning with a shared projection is more sample efficient and can improve learning on individual tasks.
- Finally, our results provide insights into the benefits of intermediate architectures that share an embedding space between task-specific layers and a backbone.

References:
[1] R. Caruana, “Multitask learning,” Machine learning , vol. 28, pp. 41–75, 1997.
[2] Y. Zhang and Q. Yang, “A survey on multi-task learning,” IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering , vol. 34, no. 12, pp. 5586–5609, 2021.
[3] T. Yu, S. Kumar, A. Gupta, S. Levine, K. Hausman, and C. Finn, “Gradient surgery for multi-task learning,” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems , vol. 33, pp. 5824–5836, 2020.
